result: The study describes the hospital setting, screening protocols, and outbreak definitions used in a geriatric hospital during the first COVID-19 pandemic wave (March-May 2020). The hospital had 196 acute-care and 100 rehabilitation beds, with up to 176 beds dedicated to COVID-19 patients. Screening protocols were implemented starting April 1, 2020, and healthcare-associated COVID-19 was defined according to Swissnoso guidelines.
evaluation: Claims C8-C14, C99-C100 provide clear methodological details about the study setting, screening protocols, and case definitions. These are straightforward descriptive claims supported by direct statements in the manuscript and adherence to established reporting guidelines (STROBE and ORION).

result: During the study period, 180 SARS-CoV-2 positive cases were identified (127 HCWs, 53 patients), with 49 nosocomial patient cases representing 20.2% of all hospitalized COVID-19 patients and 81.7% of nosocomial cases in the geriatric hospital. Ward-level attack rates ranged from 10-19% for patients and 21% for HCWs. HCWs in COVID wards had shorter delays between symptom onset and testing (mean 1.6 days) compared to HCWs in outbreak wards (mean 2.88 days).
evaluation: Claims C15-C21 present basic epidemiological data from the outbreak investigation. The proportions and attack rates are clearly stated with appropriate denominators. The difference in testing delays between HCW groups (C21) is notable and well-documented, though no statistical test is provided to assess significance.

result: Whole-genome sequencing was successfully performed on 82.2% of cases (148/180), revealing substantial genetic diversity with at least nine phylogenetic clusters. Several distinct clusters were identified, including one with 17 HCWs, 3 patients, and 6 community isolates, and another large cluster with 19 HCWs, 9 patients, and 3 community cases. Phylogenetic analysis used standard methods (MUSCLE alignment, MEGA X with Maximum Likelihood).
evaluation: Claims C22-C23 and C101-C111 describe the sequencing success rate and phylogenetic findings. The high sequencing success rate (82.2%) is well-documented, and the phylogenetic methods are standard and appropriately cited. The identification of multiple clusters with varying bootstrap support is clearly presented in Figure 2.

result: Transmission tree reconstruction identified 22 importation events (17 HCWs, 5 patients) with ≥10% posterior support, generating 41 secondary cases. When restricting to ≥50% posterior support, 16 importation events (12 HCWs, 4 patients) generated 35 secondary cases. There was uncertainty in some transmission pairs, with six pairs showing ambiguity about which case was imported versus secondary.
evaluation: Claims C24-C26, C76-C77, C112-C114 present results from the Bayesian transmission tree reconstruction using outbreaker2. The use of different posterior probability thresholds (10% and 50%) is appropriate for sensitivity analysis. The acknowledgment of uncertainty in transmission pairs (C113-C114) demonstrates appropriate caution in interpretation.

result: The transmission reconstruction model estimated high case ascertainment, with a reporting probability of 91.2% (95% CrI 86.6%-95.2%), suggesting only 8.8% of source cases were unidentified. For most cases (90.8%), the model identified direct infectors without intermediate unobserved cases. The modeling method was capable of identifying missing intermediate cases.
evaluation: Claims C27-C28, C65-C66 describe the model's performance in case ascertainment. The high reporting probability (91.2%) with narrow credible intervals suggests good surveillance coverage. The ability to identify direct transmission without intermediate cases in 90.8% of cases indicates model confidence, though this should be interpreted cautiously given the inherent uncertainty in transmission reconstruction.

result: The model's ward attribution agreed with epidemiological assessment in 95% of nosocomial cases, modifying attribution for only three patients. Patient-to-patient transmission predominantly occurred within the same ward (95.2%, 95% CrI 84.2%-100%) rather than within the same room (19.7%, 95% CrI 6.7%-33.3%). One transmission pair (C107 to C131) was predicted with 72.5% probability despite not sharing a ward.
evaluation: Claims C29-C31, C92-C94 demonstrate good concordance between epidemiological and modeling approaches. The finding that ward-level proximity was more important than room-level proximity (C30-C31) is well-supported with credible intervals. The exception case (C92-C93) is appropriately discussed with probabilities for direct versus indirect transmission.

result: Individual reproductive numbers ranged from 0 to 9 secondary infections. The proportion of non-transmitters among HCWoutbreak and nosocomial patients decreased from early (32%) to late phase (55%), suggesting reduced contribution to transmission over time. HCWcovid maintained stable non-transmitter proportions (55-60%). High transmitters (≥2 secondary cases) were more common among HCWoutbreak (28.6%) than nosocomial patients (11.8%) in late phases, though not statistically significant due to small numbers.
evaluation: Claims C32-C37, C81 describe transmission heterogeneity across case types and outbreak phases. The temporal trends are clearly presented in Figure 4. The acknowledgment that differences were not statistically significant (C37) is appropriate given small sample sizes. The interpretation about changing contributions to transmission (C34) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

result: Cases were significantly less likely than expected by chance to be infected by HCWs from COVID wards (42% observed vs. 53% expected, p=0.042), particularly among HCWs in outbreak wards (31%, p=0.07) and patients (24%, p=0.006). Conversely, HCWoutbreak were significantly more likely to be infected by other HCWoutbreak (38% vs. 18% expected, p=0.03), and nosocomial patients were more likely to be infected by other patients (56% vs. 28% expected, p=0.005).
evaluation: Claims C38-C40, C80, C96-C97 present key findings on transmission patterns with statistical testing. The comparison to random expectations is methodologically sound, and p-values are provided. The finding that HCWcovid transmission was lower than expected while HCWoutbreak and patient-to-patient transmission was higher is well-supported by the data in Figure 5.

result: Infected staff or patients in outbreak wards were responsible for significantly more transmission overall (54%, 95% CrI 48%-61%) than expected (43.7%, 95% CrI 35%-53%), driven particularly by transmission within outbreak wards (73%, 95% CrI 63%-82%). Within-ward transmission was more pronounced in outbreak wards (mean 48%, range 20-70%) than non-outbreak wards (mean 14%, range 0-63%).
evaluation: Claims C41-C42, C95 demonstrate that outbreak wards had disproportionate within-ward transmission. The credible intervals are provided and the comparison between outbreak and non-outbreak wards is clear. The findings are supported by visualizations in Appendix figures 2 and 3.

result: The combination of epidemiological and genetic data using Bayesian modeling revealed distinct transmission patterns among healthcare worker groups. HCW-to-HCW transmission in COVID wards was not higher than expected, while transmission between HCWs in non-COVID wards was twofold higher than expected. Most importation events were linked to HCWs, and transmission between HCWcovid was more limited than between patients and HCWoutbreak.
evaluation: Claims C43-C46, C73-C74 summarize the main findings about differential transmission dynamics. These conclusions are well-supported by the quantitative analyses in C38-C42. The finding that HCWcovid had lower transmission than HCWoutbreak is counterintuitive but robustly demonstrated with statistical significance.

result: The study identified excess patient-to-patient transmission occurring primarily within wards, and multiple importation events (mostly HCW-related) leading to secondary clusters. These findings highlight gaps in infection control and suggest that prevention strategies in geriatric settings should account for patient-to-patient transmission and differential transmission dynamics between HCWs in COVID versus non-COVID wards.
evaluation: Claims C47-C48, C71-C72, C75 present the study's main conclusions and implications. These are well-supported by the preceding quantitative findings (C30-C31 for patient transmission, C24-C26 for importations, C38-C46 for differential HCW dynamics). The recommendations are appropriately cautious and evidence-based.

result: The differential transmission patterns between HCW groups may be explained by behavioral factors: HCWs in COVID wards may have applied infection control measures more rigorously due to heightened concern, while HCWs in non-COVID wards may have underestimated transmission risks from peers. Supporting this, HCWs in non-COVID wards had longer presenteeism despite symptoms (mean 2.9 days) compared to COVID ward HCWs (mean 1.6 days).
evaluation: Claims C51-C54 propose behavioral explanations for observed transmission patterns. While C54 provides supporting data on presenteeism differences, C51-C53 are largely speculative. The citation to Ottolenghi et al. (C51) supports the general concept but doesn't directly validate the specific behavioral differences in this setting. These remain plausible hypotheses requiring further investigation.

result: Mathematical models suggest single-room isolation could reduce nosocomial transmission by up to 35%. In this outbreak, symptomatic patients were identified promptly (median 0-day delay), but pre-symptomatic transmission may still occur. Prior studies found that exposure to community-acquired cases (identified and segregated) carried half the risk compared to hospital-acquired cases, possibly because community-acquired patients had passed peak infectiousness upon admission.
evaluation: Claims C55-C59 cite prior literature to contextualize findings. C55-C58 are appropriately attributed to cited studies. C56 is supported by data from this study. C59 is speculative but clearly presented as a possible explanation for findings from a cited study (Mo et al., 2021). These claims appropriately distinguish between findings from this study versus prior work.

result: Current evidence does not support real-time genomics for outbreak control, and these outbreaks were controlled without using whole-genome sequencing. WGS may be more useful for ruling out transmission than confirmation due to low mutation rates between transmission pairs. However, WGS was performed on a high proportion (80%) of cases including HCWs, which has been shown to improve understanding of transmission dynamics.
evaluation: Claims C60-C63 discuss the role and limitations of WGS in outbreak investigation. C60-C62 appropriately cite literature supporting these positions. C61 is a factual statement about this outbreak. C63 accurately reports the sequencing success rate and cites supporting literature. The nuanced discussion acknowledges both the value and limitations of WGS.

result: The study collected data prospectively, minimizing bias, but was conducted during the first pandemic wave with wild-type SARS-CoV-2 in a susceptible population. Results may not be applicable to settings with high vaccination coverage or later pandemic stages, though lessons may be useful in countries with slow vaccine rollout. Nosocomial outbreaks continue to occur despite high vaccination coverage.
evaluation: Claims C64, C67-C70 discuss study strengths and limitations regarding generalizability. C64 and C67 are factual statements about study design and context. C68-C69 appropriately acknowledge limitations in generalizability while noting potential applicability. C70 is supported by citations. This represents appropriate scientific caution about external validity.

result: Transmission reconstruction used the R package outbreaker2 to combine epidemiological and genomic data. Contact networks were constructed from ward/room presence for patients and HCW shift data, with contact defined as simultaneous presence on the same ward on a given day. Formal contact tracing was limited during the study period.
evaluation: Claims C105-C107 describe the transmission reconstruction methodology. The use of outbreaker2 is well-established and appropriately cited. The contact network construction is clearly described, and the limitation of formal contact tracing is acknowledged. The definition of contact (same ward, same day) is conservative and appropriate given data limitations.

result: The introduction establishes that nosocomial SARS-CoV-2 acquisition in geriatric institutions and LTCFs accounts for large proportions of COVID-19 cases and contributes substantially to morbidity and mortality. Healthcare workers can be both victims and vectors of infection. There is ongoing controversy about HCW roles in nosocomial outbreaks, and findings from acute-care hospitals cannot be directly applied to geriatric settings. Settings caring for elderly patients have high attack rates for both patients and HCWs.
evaluation: Claims C1-C7, C49-C50 provide background context from prior literature. All claims are appropriately supported by citations to published studies. C50 specifically cites a seroprevalence study from the same hospital consortium, providing relevant local context. These claims accurately represent the state of knowledge and controversies in the field.

result: The study was supported by a grant from the Swiss National Science Foundation under the NRP78 funding scheme (Grant no. 4078P0_198363).
evaluation: Claim C98 is a straightforward statement of funding support with specific grant information. This is standard reporting practice and requires no further evaluation.
